title: Where's the post office? — directions, distance, and verb prefixes
goal: Ask for directions and understand the answer, use the third group of endings (*-hoz*, *-nál*, *-tól*), and recognize the verb prefixes that change the direction of an action.
bekal: ask for directions politely and catch a passerby's answer
use *-hoz / -nál / -tól* for people, places, and landmarks
read the prefixes *be-, ki-, fel-, le-, el-, meg-* and know when they move

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Az utcán
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost near Astoria and stops a woman walking by.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me! Where's the post office?

lines.speaker: Járókelő:
lines.text: A posta a második utcában van, balra.
lines.id: The post office is on the second street, on the left.
lines.literal: the post the second street-in is, left-to.

lines.speaker: Járókelő:
lines.text: Nem, öt perc gyalog. A gyógyszertár mellett van.
lines.id: No, five minutes on foot. It's next to the pharmacy.
lines.literal: no, five minute on-foot. the pharmacy next-to is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Köszönöm. És a metró merre van?
lines.id: Thank you. And which way is the metro?
lines.literal: I-thank. and the metro which-way is?

lines.speaker: Járókelő:
lines.text: Arra, a nagy tér felé. Az Astoriánál.
lines.id: That way, toward the big square. At Astoria.
lines.literal: that-way, the big square toward. the Astoria-at.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Is that far from the post office?

lines.speaker: Járókelő:
lines.text: Nem, két perc. Villamossal is lehet menni.
lines.id: No, two minutes. You can also take the tram.
lines.literal: no, two minute. tram-with also may go.

lines.speaker: Járókelő:
lines.text: A negyvenhetessel. A megálló ott van, a sarkon.
lines.id: The 47. The stop is over there, on the corner.
lines.literal: the forty-seven-er-with. the stop there is, the corner-on.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks a lot for your help! Bye!

notes: **Elnézést to stop someone, bocsánat to apologize.** Note that *elnézést* already carries the object ending — the full form is *Elnézést kérek* ("I ask for pardon"), and the *kérek* part is usually dropped.

**Az Astoriánál** uses the ending *-nál/-nél*, meaning "at, by, at someone's place". This group is the one used for **people and landmarks**: *az orvosnál* (at the doctor's), *Annánál* (at Anna's), *a hídnál* (by the bridge).

**Merre, arra, erre.** Three direction words that are not quite the same as *hol, ott, itt*. *Hol?* asks for a point; *Merre?* asks for a direction. The answer is *arra* (that way) or *erre* (this way), and Hungarians usually say it while pointing.
**Felé is a postposition**, so the noun stays bare: *a tér felé* (toward the square). Compare *-ra/-re*, which means all the way onto the place: *a térre megyek* (I'm going to the square).

**A negyvenhetessel.** Public transport numbers become nouns with the ending *-s*: *négy* → *négyes* (number four), *hét* → *hetes*, *negyvenhét* → *negyvenhetes*. Then they take ordinary endings: *a hetessel megyek* (I take the number seven). Everyone in Budapest talks this way.

grammars.title: The third group: people, places, landmarks
body: Unit 4 set up six endings for inside and surface. Here are the remaining three — and this is the group you must use for **people**.
after: **For people, this group is required.** *Annához megyek* (I'm going to Anna's), not *Annába* — that form means something else entirely. The same rule applies to the doctor, the barber, a friend, anyone.
**The ending -hoz has three forms**, like *-on/-en/-ön*: *az asztalhoz*, *a kerthez*, *az ördöghöz*. The third group (*ö, ő, ü, ű*) gets its own share here.
**-tól/-től also means "from" in time**, as you already used in unit 10: *kilenctől* (from nine). One ending, two jobs — and both share the same feel: a starting point.

grammars.title: Verb prefixes (igekötő)
body: A set of small words that attach to the front of a verb and sharpen its meaning. They are one of the most distinctive features of Hungarian.
after: **The prefix moves behind the verb after a negation or a question word.** *Elmegyek* (I'm leaving) → *Nem megyek el* (I'm not leaving) → *Elmegyek?* but *Mikor megyek el?*. This rule feels strange at first and quickly becomes natural, because you will hear it many times a day.

**Meg- is the most frequent and the hardest to translate.** It marks a **completed** action: *eszem a levest* (I'm eating the soup) versus *megeszem a levest* (I'll eat up the soup). English often uses "up", "through", "finish", or doesn't mark it at all.

At A1 you don't need to use these prefixes actively. What matters is **recognizing** them when they appear, so you can still find the root in a dictionary: *felkelek* is listed under *kel*, not *fel*.

grammars.title: How are you getting there?
body: Means of transport take the "with" ending; the only exception is your own two feet.
after: Note once more how the *v* merges after a consonant: *busz* → *bus**sz**al*, *vonat* → *vona**tt**al*. After a vowel it stays intact: *metró**val***, *taxi**val***.

blocks.text: Notice how many of these are built from two words you already know: *gyógyszer* (medicine) + *tár* (store), *kór* (illness) + *ház* (house), *repülő* (flyer) + *tér* (square). Hungarian hardly ever borrows a foreign word if it can build its own — that's why its vocabulary feels foreign at first and becomes surprisingly guessable later.

blocks.title: Getting around Budapest
items: The Budapest metro has four lines numbered **M1** to **M4**; M1 is the oldest underground line in continental Europe, and locals call it the *kisföldalatti* ("the little underground").

A ticket is a *jegy* and a pass is a *bérlet*. The thing to remember: tickets must be **validated** before boarding (*kezelni*), and inspectors in blue jackets often stand right at the end of the escalator.

*Átszállni* means to change (lines), *felszállni* to get on, *leszállni* to get off. All three are prefixed verbs — and the announcements on board say them many times a day, so they're some of the best free listening practice you can get.
